title: Rhian Badger and the Brilliant Mix-Up
markdown:
Dust hung in the Grand Glimmer Theatre the way flour hangs in a kitchen that has ideas. Sunlight came through the tall arched windows in pale slabs. Velvet curtains held last night’s hush. Somewhere a seat creaked, remembering an audience.

Rhian Badger stood at the heart of it with a scroll in his paws. The edges were frayed from too much careful work. He was a cartographer of uncommon patience. His maps could have guided a lost firefly through a starless wood. Today the scroll was not a map of hills. It was a plan for a Community Showcase: local talents, neatly placed, each in its proper light.

He liked proper light. He liked a key in the corner and a north arrow that told the truth. The scroll had headings in his best ink. Illumination Enhancement. Aesthetic Enhancements. Structural Reinforcement. Presentation of Contributions. He had written them as if a theatre were a parish and the parish could be surveyed.

“A cordial welcome,” he said, in the warm booming voice he used for geographical pronouncements. “We have a splendid event to prepare. Courtesy, if you please. Enthusiasm, if you have any left after the stairs.”

The volunteers milled on the dusty stage as if the dust were part of the invitation.

Professor Pipkin was a magnificently fluffy owl. Feathers escaped him the way thoughts escaped other people. He believed most problems improved after a dramatic puff of dust.

The Flutterby sisters were three iridescent butterflies who treated instructions as weather: interesting, not binding.

Bartholomew Button lurked by the ancient prop trunk. He was a stout hedgehog with a surly kindness, and he had decided, with great firmness, that this was a secret play and a loud one.

Ivy hung from a chandelier and watched, a sprightly monkey with opinions in her tail.

“Professor Pipkin,” Rhian said, unfurling the scroll. “We need illumination enhancement. All points of ingress and egress, suitably brightened. A welcoming glow.”

Pipkin’s golden eyes blinked. His head tipped, first left, then right, as if the words were a mouse he meant to catch from two directions.

“Illumination enhancement. A theatrical cue. A cascade of luminous dust to herald each entrance. Marvellous.”

He scurried toward a hidden stash of fine shimmering powder, already composing a spectacular entrance for people who had only meant to use a door.

Rhian turned to the Flutterbys, who were already investigating a cluster of potted ferns.

“Your artistic sense is needed. Aesthetic enhancements for the principal areas. Vibrant hues, if you would be so kind. A delightful day to you all.”

The sisters giggled, a sound like tiny bells that had not been asked to keep still. “Vibrant hues. For the dancers’ costumes. Dewdrop dreams on a spring morning.”

They zipped toward the costume racks. Rhian’s polite frown arrived a moment too late. He nearly called them back. The scroll, however, said the next heading was waiting, and he was a creature who finished a list.

Bartholomew shuffled closer. His prickles twitched with curiosity and gruff impatience.

“So, Mr. Badger. When do we get our lines? And why all this fuss about ambiance? My ears prefer a robust fanfare.”

Rhian let out a small puff of air. “Scripts? No. This is a showcase, not a play. The music is only a backdrop. What we need is your strength. Structural reinforcement. The temporary supports for the displays. Strong. Steady.”

Bartholomew nodded, softening a fraction. “Structural reinforcement. A castle, then. Or a mountain for acrobats.”

He began, in his mind, to stack the theatre. Rhian heard the word castle and thought, for one dangerous second, of drawing a keep on the scroll. Then he remembered he was organising chairs, not a siege, and let the hedgehog go.

The sun climbed. Long shadows crossed the floorboards. The Grand Glimmer changed, though not along any line Rhian had drawn.

Pipkin’s zeal for illumination became a dazzling fog of glitter that turned every doorway into a sparkly accident. People who tried a door immediately wondered whether they had become important. The powder smelled faintly of chalk and celebration. It got into Rhian’s whiskers and made the scroll glitter as if the parish boundaries had decided to be festive.

The Flutterbys, hearing aesthetic enhancements and seeing curtains instead of seats, painted the velvet until it hung like expensive, sticky weather. Colour ran in bright rivers and then set, glossy as boiled sweets. A fern wore a stripe of gold it had not requested.

Bartholomew, with the earnest help of six bewildered squirrels, built a precarious tower of old theatre trunks in the centre of the auditorium. The trunks smelled of moth and old programs. He stood beside the tower with his arms folded, waiting for applause that had not been scheduled.

Rhian wrung his paws. The scroll felt suddenly like a map of a country that had moved overnight.

“I asked for light,” he murmured to Ivy, “not weather. The hues were for the seating. The reinforcement was for chairs that wobble when people sit.”

Ivy’s eyes shone with the particular amusement of someone who has a good view and has chosen not to waste it. She swung once, slowly, and a flake of glitter drifted down like a wrong snow.

The showcase was due in minutes. The entertainment on offer was a glitter storm, obstructive drapery, and a trunk mountain with a proud hedgehog. Rhian’s impeccable composure frayed at the edges. He thought of all the maps he had made in quiet rooms, where rivers stayed where he put them.

Then a voice came from under a discarded velvet cushion near the orchestra pit. It was almost not a voice.

Millie was a field mouse who preferred the quiet background. Her nose twitched with the concentration of someone who had been watching the empty places while everyone else watched the spectacular mistakes.

“Excuse me, Mr. Badger?”

Rhian leaned down. His great ears did their honest work.

“You mentioned the presentation of contributions,” Millie whispered. “A central display of individual talents.”

She pointed. On the stage stood a prominent easel, entirely bare, and a conspicuously empty stretch of floor beside it. The easel had been there all morning. Rhian had walked past it twice, the way a cartographer walks past a pond that is not on the brief.

His face changed the way a map changes when you finally notice the river.

The lighting had been meant for the people and their small boards. The curtains were a backdrop, not a project. The structural work was for those boards, so they would not topple under their own proud weight. He had been so busy arranging the theatre that he had forgotten what the theatre was for.

Ivy dropped a fraction closer. “She’s right.”

Rhian crossed the dusty boards. That was the whole of it, at first: a badger walking to an empty easel. He set his scroll down. He lifted the first small display board from a heap by the wings — a watercolour of the market square, still smelling faintly of damp paper — and he fitted it onto the easel until the wooden clip held.

The empty space stopped being a mistake and became a place.

After that the volunteers moved as if they had heard a different sentence. Bartholomew’s tower came apart into a low sturdy stage of crates. The squirrels, relieved to be building something that did not lean, chattered approval. Pipkin blew his luminous dust away from the doors and left only a faint shimmer, like a polite memory of sparkle. The Flutterbys draped their least-sticky paintings behind the boards, a backdrop that knew when to stop talking.

Millie stood beside the easel. Her keen eyes helped the next board find its level: a jar of honey from the west meadow, a poem in careful pencil, a woodcarving of a duck that looked permanently surprised.

The showcase began. It was not the performance anyone had rehearsed in their heads. It was a room of small made things, each one allowed to be seen. Murmurs travelled the seats. A child pointed at the duck. An old stoat nodded at the honey as if greeting a neighbour. Applause arrived like weather that had decided to be kind.

Rhian stood a little flushed, paws still dusted with glitter that would not be mapped. Ivy swung once, gently, in the last of the window light. On the easel the market square held, slightly crooked, and did not fall.
characters: Rhian (a practical badger map maker), Ivy (a monkey friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
